doc.title: Harold Danko interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 28, 2021

title: Inventing a piano part and strumming for Thad
summary: Thad grunted approval when Danko played bell tones and strummed, becoming his signature unlike Hanna or McNeely.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. And sometimes it’ll go, like it’ll be a two staff thing with all the voicings written out, which is nice. But then it will go to some single staff with some slashes in it you know. So it’s like really, it’s one of those things where it comes down to your ears listening to it and then seeing where you might fit. With Thad I would find things where say I would come across like the band would be very tutti and then maybe I’d come across where I’d play a [hits note on piano] a bell tone, and Thad would be like [nods and grunts] you know kind of grunt. It’s like keep that in. So that became like inventing a part you know that I would play. And then when I started strumming Thad gave me a nice grunt. I think I started strumming on “That’s a Freedom,” number one in the book. That’s a Hank Jones chart. And I just started strumming four to the bar because there was no guitar there. And Thad grunted, mmm, keep that in. So that became like a little signature that I did that Roland Hanna before me, and nobody did, and Jim McNeely after me didn’t do. So that little thing that I did that got the grunts, like keep that in, because it just maybe reminded him of maybe the early days of the band you know.
